key_patterns.name: Heterogeneous risk-driven adoption
key_patterns.description: Agents with higher risk_perception are more likely to wear masks initially and adopt sooner post-exposure.
key_patterns.relevance: Set individual susceptibility and initial adoption probabilities; stratify calibration by risk_perception quantiles.

key_patterns.name: Layered diffusion with strong family influence
key_patterns.description: Family ties are few but strong; work/school are moderate; community is broad but weaker per tie.
key_patterns.relevance: Weight influence by layer; prioritize family transmissions for early cascades.

key_patterns.name: Complex contagion behavior
key_patterns.description: Adoption probability rises nonlinearly with the fraction/number of adopting neighbors; multiple exposures often precede adoption.
key_patterns.relevance: Use threshold or logistic-with-saturation functions rather than simple independent transmission.

key_patterns.name: Information precedes adoption
key_patterns.description: received_info typically becomes true before wearing_mask; adoption hazard is higher after info arrival.
key_patterns.relevance: Model a two-stage process (info diffusion → behavior adoption) with distinct parameters.

key_patterns.name: Churn and partial reversions
key_patterns.description: Some agents drop mask-wearing after adopting; churn is lower when neighbor adoption remains high.
key_patterns.relevance: Include retention dynamics modulated by local social norms.

key_patterns.name: Homophily and clustering by age_group/occupation
key_patterns.description: Ties concentrate within the same age_group and occupation, especially in work/school and family layers.
key_patterns.relevance: Expect cluster-level cascades and unequal adoption across groups; calibrate group-specific parameters.

key_patterns.name: Early influencer concentration
key_patterns.description: Early adopters often have higher degree or overlap ties across multiple layers with the same alters.
key_patterns.relevance: When seeding or estimating Rb, account for degree and multiplex overlap.

key_distributions.name: Degree distribution per layer
key_distributions.description: family: low-degree, narrow; work_school: medium, possibly right-skewed; community: right-skewed/heavy-tailed.
key_distributions.parameters: For each layer L: mean_degree_L, variance_degree_L, tail index (if heavy-tailed).

key_distributions.name: Risk perception
key_distributions.description: Continuous 0–1; typically modeled well by a Beta distribution.
key_distributions.parameters: Fit Beta(α, β) to risk_perception; also compute quantiles (Q20, Q50, Q80).

key_distributions.name: Adoption latency
key_distributions.description: Time from first information exposure (or first neighbor adoption exposure) to adoption; right-skewed.
key_distributions.parameters: Lognormal or geometric: lognormal(μ, σ) in steps; or geometric(p_adopt_per_step).

key_distributions.name: Exposures-to-adoption
key_distributions.description: Number of adopting-neighbor exposure events before first adoption.
key_distributions.parameters: Negative binomial NB(r, p) or geometric with mean_exposures_before_adoption.

key_distributions.name: Churn (time-to-drop)
key_distributions.description: Duration from adoption to first drop; decreases with higher neighbor adoption.
key_distributions.parameters: Exponential/geometric baseline with rate λ_drop; modulated by local adoption.

key_distributions.name: Assortativity by adoption
key_distributions.description: Positive assortativity expected due to homophily and local norm reinforcement.
key_distributions.parameters: Newman assortativity coefficient r_adopt in [-1, 1] over the multiplex or per layer.

key_relationships.relationship: Positive association; higher risk_perception increases initial adoption probability.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate via logistic regression; expect moderate-to-strong (OR > 1.5 per +0.25 risk).

key_relationships.relationship: Receipt of information increases next-step adoption hazard.
key_relationships.strength: Quantify as hazard ratio; expect HR > 2 controlling for social exposure.

key_relationships.relationship: Nonlinear increasing function with threshold-like effects; concave after saturation.
key_relationships.strength: Fit spline or logistic with quadratic term; strong local effect within family layer.

key_relationships.relationship: Group differences in adoption trajectories (e.g., students vs white collar).
key_relationships.strength: Test via interaction terms; expected medium differences; use for inequality_of_adoption.

key_relationships.relationship: Higher degree correlates with earlier adoption and higher influence count.
key_relationships.strength: Partial correlation controlling for risk_perception; expected moderate.

variables: multiplex overlap (same pair in multiple layers)
key_relationships.relationship: Overlapped ties increase influence per dyad.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate as per-dyad multiplier > 1.2 relative to single-layer ties.

initial_adoption_rate.notes: Compute p0 = sum_1{wearing_mask_day0}/N. Use exact seeds from day 0 when possible.

initial_informed_rate.notes: Initialize information state; if missing day 0, use earliest observed day.

seed_selection_method.value: Use observed day-0 mask wearers as seeds; if synthetic run, sample seeds proportional to degree*risk_perception
seed_selection_method.notes: Preserves empirically plausible early influencer profile.

layer_influence_weights.notes: Relative weights per contact; calibrate by matching early Rb and adoption latency.

layer_contact_probabilities_per_step.notes: Probability of interacting with each neighbor per step; tune with exposure counts vs observed adoption timing.

edge_directionality.notes: Symmetrize edges and deduplicate per layer.

homophily_by_group.notes: Quantify as ratio of within-group edges to random-mixing expectation; used if generating or rewiring networks.

adoption_hazard_model.value: logit(p_adopt_it) = α + β1*frac_neighbors_adopt_it-1 + β2*(frac_neighbors_adopt_it-1)^2 + β3*received_info_it-1 + β4*risk_perception_i + β5*(risk_perception_i * frac_neighbors_adopt_it-1) + Σ_L γ_L*frac_neighbors_adopt_in_layer_L_it-1
adoption_hazard_model.notes: Fit via discrete-time hazard regression; include agent random effects if sufficient data.

complex_contagion_threshold.source: exposures-before-adoption derived from time series and network
complex_contagion_threshold.notes: Alternative to logistic: agent adopts when cumulative weighted exposures exceed K_i ~ Poisson(λ). Calibrate λ to match mean_exposures_before_adoption.

info_diffusion.notes: Two channels: social (neighbors) and exogenous. Fit via hazard model on received_info.

adoption_delay_distribution.source: time difference between info/exposure and adoption
adoption_delay_distribution.notes: Represents cognitive/behavioral delay after threshold is met.

drop_hazard.value: logit(p_drop_it) = δ0 + δ1*(1 - frac_neighbors_adopt_it-1) + δ2*(1 - risk_perception_i)
drop_hazard.notes: Expect δ1 > 0; calibrate to match adoption_churn_rate and persistence curves.

multiplex_overlap_multiplier.source: dyads connected in multiple layers vs single layer influence
multiplex_overlap_multiplier.notes: Multiply exposure weight if the same dyad exists in ≥2 layers.

exposure_window.source: fit to maximize predictive power of lagged neighbor adoption for current adoption
exposure_window.notes: Number of past steps to aggregate exposures for adoption/churn decisions.

mandate_effect.source: if known mandate dates; otherwise scenario parameter
mandate_effect.notes: Apply from policy start day; estimate by difference-in-differences if event exists in data.

targeting_rules.value: If campaign: prioritize low-risk_perception and low-adoption groups (age_group/occupation) with highest betweenness centrality
targeting_rules.notes: Optimizes cascade size subject to budget.

Rb_window.notes: Compute behavior reproduction number over first 3 steps after adoption events.

convergence_threshold.notes: Convergence when |adoption_rate_t - adoption_rate_t-1| < threshold for 5 consecutive steps.

preprocessing_steps.step: Parse agent_attributes.csv; cast agent_id to int; standardize categorical levels for age_group and occupation.
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Initialize agent traits and subgroup labels.

preprocessing_steps.step: Load social_network.json; convert keys to int; deduplicate adjacency lists; enforce undirected edges per layer.
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Build multiplex graph with clean layer-specific neighbor sets.

preprocessing_steps.step: Load time series; parse booleans; ensure uniqueness of (day, agent_id); identify earliest day as baseline.
Merge datasets by agent_id; drop or impute agents missing in any file; flag isolated agents per layer.
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Create a unified panel for analysis and simulation initialization.

preprocessing_steps.step: Compute per-step neighbor exposure features: fraction and count of adopting neighbors per layer and overall; include multiplex overlap indicator.
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Construct predictors for hazard and threshold estimation.

preprocessing_steps.step: Detect transition times: first received_info day, first adoption day, first drop day.
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Enable latency, hazard, and churn estimation.

preprocessing_steps.step: Estimate network diagnostics: degree distributions per layer, clustering coefficients, assortativity by age_group/occupation.
preprocessing_steps.purpose: Inform layer weights and homophily parameters.

preprocessing_steps.step: Calculate group-level adoption time series by age_group and occupation.

calibration_strategy.calibration_approach: Use a two-stage estimation plus simulation-based refinement. Stage 1: Fit discrete-time hazard models. (A) received_info_t ~ lagged neighbor info/adoption and exogenous trend. (B) wearing_mask_t ~ lagged neighbor adoption (overall and per layer), received_info, risk_perception, and interactions; include random effects if data permits. Estimate parameters (α, β, γ, δ) and derive implied thresholds and delays. Stage 2: Initialize simulation with observed day-0 states and run forward using estimated parameters. Perform multi-objective optimization (e.g., Bayesian optimization or CMA-ES/ABC) to minimize distance between simulated and observed metrics: adoption_rate_over_time, mean_exposures_before_adoption, adoption_churn_rate, behavior_reproduction_number_Rb (early window), and assortativity_by_adoption trajectory. Use priors from Stage 1 and penalize deviation from fitted coefficients to avoid overfitting.
calibration_strategy.validation_strategy: Temporal cross-validation: fit on first 60–70% of days, validate on the remainder. Posterior predictive checks for all evaluation metrics. Hold out subgroups (e.g., one occupation) or ego-nets to test generalization. Compare observed vs simulated: (1) adoption_rate_over_time (RMSE), (2) time_to_50_percent_adoption, (3) Rb during early growth (t=1..Rb_window), (4) churn curves (survival of adoption), (5) mean_exposures_before_adoption distribution (KS statistic), (6) assortativity_by_adoption trend, and (7) inequality_of_adoption across age_group/occupation. Perform sensitivity analysis on layer_influence_weights and exposure_window; report parameter elasticities.
key_variables_to_calibrate: adoption_hazard_model coefficients (α, β1, β2, β3, β4, β5, γ_L)

file_summaries:
Semantic metadata summary for agent_attributes.csv

- Data structure and type
  - CSV; flat, rectangular table.
  - One row per agent; no nesting. Suitable for direct load into a DataFrame or dict of agents.

- Columns and meanings
  - agent_id (int): Unique agent identifier; primary key for joins (e.g., to network edges).
  - age_group (categorical): Demographic cohort (e.g., Youth, Young Adult, Middle Age); can proxy for norms, susceptibility, and contact patterns.
  - occupation (categorical): Role/environment (e.g., Student, Blue Collar, White Collar); informs daily context and network layer (school, workplace, community).
  - risk_perception (float 0–1): Agent-specific perceived risk level; higher values indicate greater concern/aversion to infection.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - None within the file; each row is independent.
  - Intended external relationships: agent_id links to social network edges or location schedules; age_group/occupation define subgroup memberships and homophily.

- How this data informs the simulation
  - Agent initialization
    - Create agents keyed by agent_id; attach age_group, occupation, risk_perception traits.
    - Optionally derive initial mask_wearing state with P(mask_0) = f(risk_perception, age_group, occupation).
  - Decision dynamics
    - risk_perception modulates adoption threshold/sensitivity to social influence and public signals.
    - age_group and occupation can set baseline compliance, influence weights, and responsiveness heterogeneity.
  - Network/interaction structure
    - occupation maps agents to interaction layers (school vs workplace) and degree distributions.
    - age_group and occupation drive homophily for tie formation and layer-specific contact rates.
  - Policy/experiment hooks
    - Targeted interventions by subgroup (e.g., students) or by risk_perception quantiles.
    - Shock updates to risk_perception from information campaigns; track behavior diffusion conditioned on these attributes.

Semantic metadata summary for social_network.json

- Overall structure and type:
  - JSON object representing a multiplex (multi-layer) social network.
  - Top-level is a dictionary keyed by agent IDs (as strings), each mapping to an object with three adjacency lists.

- Meaning of keys/columns:
  - Top-level keys (e.g., "0", "1", "2"): unique agent identifiers (convertible to integers).
  - Nested keys:
    - family: list of agent IDs connected via household/familial ties.
    - work_school: list of agent IDs connected via workplace/school ties.
    - community: list of agent IDs connected via broader community ties (neighbors, friends, social groups).

- Relationships and nested elements:
  - Each agent has up to three lists of neighbors, one per layer. Lists are unweighted and imply presence of a tie in that context.
  - The network is layer-specific; the same pair may or may not appear in multiple layers.
  - Directionality is not explicit; treat edges as undirected if reciprocity is enforced in the full file, otherwise as directed or symmetrize during preprocessing.
  - IDs in lists reference other agents in the same global index space.

- How this informs simulation entities/interactions:
  - Agents: instantiate one agent per top-level key with state variables (e.g., mask_wearing: bool/probability; susceptibility to influence; layer-specific conformity).
  - Layers/contexts: model three interaction contexts with different contact frequencies and influence strengths (e.g., family > work_school > community for tie strength).
  - Interaction scheduling: at each time step, sample contacts from each layer per agent using layer-specific rates; propagate mask-wearing via social influence along listed ties.
  - Influence mechanics: assign layer weights or transmission probabilities per layer; optionally different thresholds or reinforcement if multiple layers connect the same pair.
  - Preprocessing notes: convert keys to ints; ensure neighbor IDs exist; deduplicate per list; decide on undirected vs directed handling; allow agents with empty lists in some layers.

- Data structure and type: Flat CSV time series. Each row is a snapshot of an individual agent’s state on a specific day. Composite key (day, agent_id). Boolean-like fields use true/false strings.
- Columns and meanings:
  - day (int): Discrete simulation time step.
  - agent_id (int): Unique identifier for an agent; stable across days.
  - wearing_mask (bool): Agent’s behavioral state (mask adoption) on that day.
  - received_info (bool): Whether the agent has received mask-related information by that day.
- Relationships/nesting: No nested elements; relationships are temporal per agent across days. Events are state transitions:
  - Information acquisition: received_info changes false→true (and possibly back if non-monotonic).
  - Behavior adoption: wearing_mask changes false→true (and possibly back).
  - The earliest true per agent marks first adoption/info times.
- Implications for the simulation:
  - Initialize agents at day 0 using the first-day rows (seed mask wearers and informed agents).
  - Use longitudinal transitions to estimate/calidate mechanisms:
    - Info diffusion rate (hazard of received_info becoming true).
    - Adoption conditional on info and/or social influence (P[w_t+1 | received_info, peers]).
    - Persistence/decay if reversions exist.
  - Lacks explicit network topology; supply or infer a network separately (e.g., synthetic graph) and calibrate parameters so simulated time series match observed transitions.
  - Treat (day, agent_id) as unique; ensure booleans parsed correctly; detect and timestamp transitions for learning and validation.
